1.title: Understand how investment in AI works
1.intro: An investment firm puts money into companies; an AI focus means judging data, models and teams.
pts: Stages: seed, early, growth. Each has different risk and information.
Money comes from limited partners; managers owe them honest reports.
AI companies differ: tools, applications, data, services. Judge whether the data or the model is the real asset.
Write a one-page thesis: what we back, why now, what we avoid.
Read one real company's public filings or website and list five claims you can check and five you cannot.
1.ex: Thesis: 'We back applied AI for Canadian clinics and logistics at seed stage; we avoid pure model-building without data access.'
1.act: Write a thesis and test it against three real companies' public information.

2.title: Know the securities rules
2.intro: Raising and investing money is regulated.
pts: Provincial securities regulators govern who may raise funds, give advice and sell investments; exemptions exist for some investors.
Managers may need registration; do not act before checking.
Anti-money-laundering rules require identifying investors and sources of funds.
Marketing must be balanced; never promise returns.
Check that you can lawfully see the information you use; do not trade on private information.
2.ex: Row: 'Raise a fund from friends | provincial securities regulator | check exemption and registration | before any pitch | lawyer's written opinion'.
2.act: Build a rules table for a small fund and ask a licensed adviser to review.

3.title: Evaluate an AI company
pts: Check the data: source, rights to use, quality and bias.
Check the model: accuracy on held-out data, cost to run, drift over time.
Check the team and customers: paid pilots count more than letters of intent.
Write findings in a short memo with a rating and open questions.
Ask what the company would do with money, by when, and how you would know it worked.
3.ex: Claim '95% accuracy' tested on the company's own test set; independent sample shows 84%. Memo rating drops from strong to watch.
3.act: Review one public AI company and write a two-page memo.
3.std: Each claim has evidence or is marked unverified.

4.title: Model returns and fees
pts: A fund of 10,000,000 with 2% yearly fee costs 200,000 a year.
Returns come from a few big winners; most investments return little.
Model three cases: poor, expected, strong.
Be clear about fees and carried interest.
Compare fund costs over ten years with a fee table, not a feeling.
4.ex: Invest 500,000 across 10 companies at 50,000 each. Outcomes: 6 return nothing, 3 return 50,000 each, 1 returns 400,000 (8x). Total back = 150,000 + 400,000 = 550,000, which is 1.1x before fees. Teaching figures: one big winner decides the result.

5.title: Manage the portfolio
pts: Quarterly review: revenue, cash, hires, risks.
Reserve money for follow-on rounds.
Set triggers for support or exit.
Report to investors in a fixed format.
Record why you made each decision on the day, so you can learn later.
5.ex: Quarter page: 10 companies, 2 behind plan, 1 needing a bridge; action: reserve 200,000.
5.act: Build a quarterly dashboard for a fictional portfolio.
5.std: Every company has a status and next step.

6.title: Source and win deals
pts: Network with universities, accelerators and founders.
Give founders fast, clear answers.
Offer help beyond money: introductions and advice.
Track deal flow: seen, met, diligence, offer, closed.
Keep a list of founders you met and notes for follow-up, with their consent.
6.ex: Funnel: 120 seen, 30 met, 8 diligence, 3 offers, 2 closed.
6.act: Run a deal funnel for 4 weeks (public companies or case studies).

7.title: Handle AI ethics and conflicts
pts: Screen for harmful uses and biased data.
Declare conflicts of interest.
Respect privacy law (PIPEDA) in portfolio companies.
Publish an investment policy.
Write the policy for what you do if a founder behaves badly.
7.ex: Policy line: 'We do not back face-recognition used without consent.'
7.act: Write a one-page responsible investing policy.
7.std: Policy has screens and a review step.

8.title: Pilot a mock fund
pts: Pick 5 public companies and a thesis.
Track for 60 days with notes.
Compare with a simple benchmark.
Write a review: what the thesis got right and wrong.
Keep your paper fund simple: no more than five names.
8.ex: Paper portfolio +3% vs benchmark +1%; reason noted: luck vs thesis.
8.act: Run the paper fund and present the review.
